notes.meaning: God tells Moses to give Israel these civil laws, which are case-by-case rules to help judges decide disputes. Since God was their king, these rulings set up a fair and orderly society based on natural justice. They also put the Ten Commandments into daily practice, especially how people ought to treat their neighbors.

A fellow Hebrew who fell into debt, poverty, or crime could sell his services, but he could only be held for six years. In the seventh year, his master had to release him freely without charging him any money. This law kept slavery among God's people within strict limits, treating it as temporary indentured work rather than permanent ownership.
If a man entered servitude single, he left single when his time was done. If he arrived already married to a Hebrew woman, she went out free with him because she was not the master's possession.

If the master gave the servant a female slave as a wife and they had children, the wife and children stayed with the master when the man's six years ended. Because the woman was already the master's property, her children remained under his care and ownership. The man alone received his release at the end of his term.

A servant who loved his master and did not want to leave his wife and children could choose to stay. The master brought him before the judges to make an open declaration, and then pierced his ear against a door or doorpost with an awl. This ceremony marked him as a willing bond-servant who chose to stay in that home for the rest of his life.

A father in extreme poverty could place his daughter into a household, usually with the expectation that she would become a wife to the master or his son. For this reason, she did not simply leave after six years like an ordinary hired servant. Her place was protected as a family member rather than treated as field labor.

If the master changed his mind and decided not to take her as his wife, he was considered to have broken faith with her. He was not permitted to sell her to foreigners or strangers. Instead, he had to allow her family to buy her back and set her free.

If the master gave the young woman to his son to be a wife, he was required to treat her with the dignity of his own daughter. She was no longer to be viewed as a maid, but was to receive a daughter's family standing and dowry.

If the man took a second wife, he was forbidden from cutting back the first wife's food, her clothing, or her marital rights. Even when plural marriage was permitted under ancient customs, a husband was not allowed to neglect or mistreat his first wife.

If the family failed to provide the woman with food, clothing, and her full marriage rights, she was given complete freedom right away. Her owner could not demand any money for her release, protecting her from being kept in a home that dishonored her.

A person who strikes someone and causes their death must be put to death. This law rests on God's ancient command that human life is made in His image and must be protected by the civil courts. Society has a duty to punish murder so that innocent blood is not treated lightly.

God makes a clear distinction between deliberate murder and accidental death where there was no plan to harm. In an accidental death, which happens under God's mysterious providence, the killer was not guilty of murder. God promised to provide special places of safety, later called cities of refuge, where that person could flee from angry relatives.

If someone planned ahead to murder a neighbor with trickery and malice, no place was safe for him. The magistrates were ordered to drag the killer away even from God's sacred altar to face execution. God's house was meant to be a place of holy worship, not a hideout for wicked criminals.

Anyone who physically attacks their mother or father must be put to death. Striking a parent was seen as a dreadful rebellion against the family and against God Himself, who gave parents their authority. This severe penalty guarded the respect and safety that children owe to their elders.

Kidnapping a human being carried the death penalty, whether the person had already been sold into slavery or was still in the kidnapper's hands. Stealing a person destroys the freedom that makes human life valuable. God viewed slave-trading through kidnapping as a crime equal to murder.

A person who curses their father or mother was also condemned to death. This was not just a rude word dropped in a hurry, but an open, hateful wish for a parent's ruin or death. God takes deep offense at children who reject their parents with contempt and malice.

If two men fight and one injures the other so that he is stuck in bed, the attacker is spared the death penalty once the victim recovers enough to walk outside with a cane. However, the attacker was not off the hook. He had to pay for the victim's lost working wages and cover the entire cost of medical care until he was fully healed.

While ancient law allowed masters to discipline servants with a rod, beating a servant to death was punishable by law. This showed that servants were human beings with rights under God, not mere property. If the servant lived for a day or two before dying, the master was not executed for murder, because the delay showed there was no intent to kill, and the owner suffered the financial loss of his servant.

If men are fighting and accidentally strike a pregnant woman, causing the baby to come early without lasting harm, the striker was fined. The woman's husband asked for damages for the danger and pain, and the judges set a fair amount. Even when an injury was accidental, God held people responsible for the trouble they caused.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note the ancient Greek translation read this as a fine if the baby was not yet fully formed, while many modern readers take the verse as describing a miscarriage where only the mother's survival prevents a murder charge.

notes.meaning: If serious lasting injury or death followed the blow, the court had to demand an exact punishment: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, and a wound for a wound. This rule gave judges a standard of strict justice so the penalty matched the crime. It was designed to keep people from taking wild, out-of-control personal revenge.

differ.view: The Baptist tradition emphasizes that Jesus replaced this civil principle of retaliation with a higher standard of personal mercy and forgiveness in Matthew 5:38.
The Reformed tradition distinguishes between private revenge, which Christ forbade, and the civil magistrate's duty to punish crimes with fair, proportional penalties.

notes.meaning: A master was not allowed to mistreat his servants with violence. If an owner struck a servant and destroyed an eye or knocked out a tooth, that servant had to be given immediate freedom. This law taught masters to show restraint, because a single cruel blow meant losing the servant completely.

If an ox gored a person to death, the animal had to be stoned, and its meat could not be eaten or sold. This total loss reminded everyone of how precious human life is in the eyes of God. As long as the animal had never shown dangerous behavior before, the owner was not blamed for the tragedy.

If the ox was already known to gore people and the owner had been warned but failed to lock it up, the owner was held guilty of death if someone was killed. Neglecting an obvious danger made the owner responsible for the loss of life. However, the court could allow the owner to buy back his life by paying a heavy fine set by the family and the judges.

The same legal rule applied whether the goring ox killed a grown adult or a neighbor's son or daughter. If the animal killed a servant, the owner had to pay thirty pieces of silver to the servant's master to replace his loss, and the ox was still stoned. Human life was treated with deep honor in every case.

A person who dug a pit or uncovered an old cistern and left it open was held responsible if an animal fell in and died. The person who caused the danger had to pay full money value to the owner, and in return he kept the dead animal's meat and hide. God's law teaches us that careless neglect that harms a neighbor must be put right.

If one man's ox fought with and killed another's, and neither animal had a history of violence, the loss was shared equally. Both owners sold the live animal, split the money, and divided the dead meat. This fair compromise made sure that an unexpected accident did not crush either neighbor alone.

If the ox was known to be violent in the past and the owner failed to pen it up, that owner had to pay for the full value of a living animal. The owner received the dead carcass, but he had to give an ox for an ox to the victim. Knowing about a danger and failing to stop it leaves a person fully accountable for the damage.
